1111.quote_or_event: “You are the Emperor, and I call You a chief - how does this add to Your greatness?”
1111.explanation: In Raag Bilaval, Guru Nanak says that any praise he can give the Lord falls short, like calling an emperor a mere chief.
1111.tie_back: The Kural praises the anicham flower as soft, then says the beloved is softer still; Guru Nanak likewise says every comparison falls short of the Beloved.
1111.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 795, Raag Bilaval, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1111._accuracy_note: Next-best match: both say the beloved goes beyond any comparison, but Guru Nanak is speaking of the inadequacy of praising God, with no flower or physical softness involved.

1112.quote_or_event: “I can see no other as great as You; O Lord of Wisdom, You are pleasing to my mind.”
1112.explanation: In Raag Gauri, Guru Ram Das tells the Lord that nothing else he sees can stand beside Him, and that He alone delights his mind.
1112.tie_back: The Kural's lover tells his heart that common flowers, which anyone may look at, are no match for his beloved's eyes; Guru Ram Das also refuses to set anything beside the One he loves.
1112.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 305, Raag Gauri, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1112._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the incomparability of the beloved is shared, but the Gurbani verse is devotion to God and has nothing of the Kural's flower-and-eyes comparison.

1113.quote_or_event: “Your eyes are so beautiful, and Your teeth are delightful. Your nose is so graceful, and Your hair is so long. Your body is so precious, cast in gold.”
1113.explanation: In a Vadhans chhant, Guru Nanak describes the beauty of the Lord feature by feature (eyes, teeth, nose, hair and a body like gold), while the Sikh commentators note that all beauty in creation is His.
1113.tie_back: The Kural lists the beloved's body, smile, fragrance, eyes and shoulders, each with its classic comparison; Guru Nanak gives the same kind of feature-by-feature praise of the Beloved.
1113.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 567, Raag Vadhans, Chhant, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1113._accuracy_note: Close match in form, a catalogue of the beloved's features; the beauty praised is that of the formless Lord seen in creation, which is spiritual, not romantic, love.

1114.quote_or_event: “In the Fear of God, the sun shines, and in the Fear of God, the moon reflects.”
1114.explanation: In Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak describes the whole of nature, sun, moon, wind and water, as moving in awe of God.
1114.tie_back: The Kural imagines the water-lilies bowing their heads in shame before the beloved's eyes; Guru Nanak pictures all of nature humbled in awe before God.
1114.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 464, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1114._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the shared picture is nature bowing before something greater, but the Guru's point is God's hukam (order) over creation, not a flower outdone by a woman's eyes.

1115.quote_or_event: “Your eyes are so beautiful, and Your teeth are delightful.”
1115.explanation: No passage in Gurbani matches this kural's playful hyperbole about a waist too delicate to bear flower stalks; the nearest Sikh parallel is Guru Nanak's Vadhans chhant, which praises the Beloved's beauty in loving detail.
1115.tie_back: The Kural exaggerates the beloved's delicacy for comic effect; Gurbani shares only the loving attention to the Beloved's beauty, not the joke.
1115.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 567, Raag Vadhans, Chhant, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1115._accuracy_note: Weak, next-best match: Sikh scripture has nothing like this comic hyperbole about a fragile waist, and the line repeats the source used for kural 1113.

1116.quote_or_event: “In the bowl of the sky, the sun and moon are the lamps; the stars in the constellations are the pearls.”
1116.explanation: In his Aarti, Guru Nanak pictures the whole sky as a worship tray, with the sun, moon and stars arranged in praise of the Lord.
1116.tie_back: In the Kural the stars are thrown into confusion because the beloved's face looks like a second moon; Guru Nanak too puts the moon and stars in the service of the Beloved.
1116.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 663, Raag Dhanasari, Aarti, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1116._accuracy_note: Next-best only: both use the moon and stars to honour the beloved, but the Aarti is cosmic worship of God, and nothing in it matches the stars' confusion.

1117.quote_or_event: “He has no stain, so I have no pollution.”
1117.explanation: In Raag Asa, Guru Arjan says the Lord is untouched by any stain of Maya, and the devotee who belongs to Him becomes stainless too.
1117.tie_back: The Kural says the moon carries a spot but the beloved's face has none; Guru Arjan calls the Beloved Lord wholly without stain.
1117.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 391, Raag Asa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1117._accuracy_note: Next-best match: the stainless beloved is shared, but Gurbani speaks of moral and spiritual purity (God as Niranjan, untouched by Maya), not physical flawlessness, and there is no moon in the verse.

1118.quote_or_event: “Millions of moons twinkle in the sky.”
1118.explanation: In Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir lists the vast powers that serve the Lord, among them millions of moons that give light at His door, as the Punjabi commentators explain.
1118.tie_back: The Kural tells the moon it would be loved only if it could shine like the beloved's face; Kabir's Lord is so radiant that millions of moons are merely His lamps.
1118.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1162, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1118._accuracy_note: Next-best only: both put the moon below the beloved's radiance, but Kabir's verse is about God's majesty, and the sense of moons as lamps at His door comes from the commentary, not the English line.

1119.quote_or_event: “The Gurmukh sees Him with intuitive ease.”
1119.explanation: In Raag Gauri, Guru Nanak says the Lord, hidden from most people, is seen naturally by the Gurmukh, the one who follows the Guru.
1119.tie_back: The Kural asks the moon not to shine for all to see, since the beloved's face is seen by the lover alone; in Gurbani the Beloved also stays hidden from the many and is seen by the one who loves Him through the Guru.
1119.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 222, Raag Gauri, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1119._accuracy_note: Weak, next-best match: Gurbani teaches that God is present everywhere and can be seen by anyone who turns to the Guru, which only loosely matches the Kural's wish that the beloved be seen by one person alone.

1120.quote_or_event: “Fareed, the path is muddy, and the house of my Beloved is so far away.”
1120.explanation: In his saloks, Sheikh Farid describes the lover hesitating at a muddy lane on the way to the Beloved's house; the following lines (paraphrased) weigh a soaked blanket against a broken heart, and he chooses to go.
1120.tie_back: The Kural pictures feet so delicate that even swan's down feels like thorns; Farid also dwells on the hardships of the lover's path, though for him love makes the rough road worth walking.
1120.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1120._accuracy_note: Weak, next-best match: Gurbani has no praise of the beloved's delicate feet; Farid shares only the theme of the hard road beneath the lover's feet, and his love is spiritual, not romantic.
